title: Getting started: hosted generation, streams and robustness
summary: Redwood AE + SE walked BrightScale through hosted generation basics: streaming response shapes, key params and tradeoffs, and resiliency patterns (retries, exponential backoff, model fallbacks). Customer focused on latency/cost tradeoffs and data controls; asked for benchmarks on their prompt set and security docs. Next steps agreed: share quickstart + pricing, run latency test with customer's prompts, and schedule pilot kickoff call.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-10
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Liam Chen (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (BrightScale CTO), Jon Meyer (ML Engineer), Priya Singh (Eng Mgr)
Links shared: Quickstart deck https://redwood.ai/quickstarts/hosted-gen, Security whitepaper link noted to be shared

[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick roll call?
[00:05] Aisha (BrightScale - CTO): Hi, Aisha here. Jon and Priya are with me. thanks Maya.
[00:12] Jon (BrightScale - ML Eng): Jon here. excited to see the hosted flow.
[00:16] Priya (BrightScale - Eng Mgr): Priya, hi.
[00:20] Maya: Great. I'll hand off to Liam for the technical walkthrough but I'll kick us off with context: BrightScale is evaluating hosted inference for a chat-assist feature. primary concerns are predictable latency, cost per token and ease of integrating retries/failover. sound right?
[00:35] Aisha: Yep, that's it. also we have SOC 2 requirements and we need to know how logs and request data are retained.
[00:42] Liam (Redwood SE): Great, we'll cover that. Quick agenda: 1) hosted API overview and generation params, 2) streaming demo and what you see on the wire, 3) retry/backoff and fallbacks, 4) brief on security and next steps.

[01:05] Liam: So hosted endpoint looks like a standard REST or SDK call. you POST a chat object, we return chunks if you enable streaming. by default streaming is off, you can flip it on with stream=true.
[01:22] Jon: When you stream, is that SSE? websockets? how's the connection?
[01:28] Liam: We support server-sent events for quick integration, plus SDK streaming helpers. websockets are not required for the hosted API right now. the streaming chunks are incremental deltas that include token text and finish_reason when it's done.
[01:45] Priya: what about partial token cost accounting while streaming? does bill happen only at finish?
[01:50] Liam: Billing is by token consumed; you see estimated tokens as they stream but final token charge is computed when the response completes. there can be slight differences due to tokenizer quirks.

[02:15] Maya: Quick demo — Liam will call the hosted chat endpoint with a sample user prompt. Liam, do you want to share your screen?
[02:21] Liam: Yep, sharing. okay here's a curl sample and python SDK snippet. I'm going to call model: rwd-small-v1 as a lightweight example.
[02:33] [02:33] Liam (screen): curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/chat \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer <redacted>' \
  -d '{"stream": true, "messages": [{"role":"user","content":"Summarize the onboarding steps for a new user in one paragraph."}]}'
[02:55] [02:55] Liam: you should see chunked messages arriving, each with a delta. sometimes the transcriber in our tools shows 'K-V cash' instead of KV cache, so ignore that in the transcript haha.

[03:10] [03:10] Maya: while Liam runs that, a couple of parameters to call out: temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop sequences, and presence/penalty. temperature controls randomness, top_p is nucleus sampling. lower temp -> more deterministic.
[03:29] Jon: For production chat we want consistent outputs more than creative so we're leaning lower temp. what range do you recommend?
[03:34] Liam: For assistant style, start with temp 0.0-0.3. if you need variety, bump to 0.6. Top_p is useful too; often teams keep top_p at 0.9 and temp at 0.2.

[04:00] [04:00] Liam (screen): here's the streaming output — chunk 1, chunk 2, finish_reason: stop. you can see the delta structure: {"type":"delta","text":"Summarize the onboarding..."} and then a final object with usage.tokens. small demo complete.
[04:20] Aisha: Looks clean. what about retry patterns? we have intermittent 5xxs from other providers and we want a recommended approach.
[04:28] Liam: Good question. We recommend an idempotent design for short generation calls; use exponential backoff with jitter. typical pattern: retry up to 3 times with base backoff 200ms, 2x multiplier, jitter +-100ms. but for streaming calls, if you lose the connection mid-stream you should attempt a ranged request using the prefix you received — we provide a resume token capability in the SDK, or you can fall back to a lower-cost non-streaming call.
[05:00] Jon: Resume token? can you expand on that?
[05:03] Liam: Sure. in the SDK we expose a resume_cursor (simple offset of generated tokens) so you can re-request starting from that token position; that reduces re-computation. it's not perfect with some models if you change params, but for same model/config it's reliable. sometimes docs show it as "resume_cursor" or "resume_offset" — sorry transcription tends to mangle.

[05:30] Priya: If we do resume and the model variant isn't available (e.g., rwd-small saturated), do you have automatic fallback to another variant?
[05:36] Liam: Yes — smart routing can optionally fallback. policy options: strict (no fallback), cost-priority (prefer cheaper variants with same semantics), or latency-priority (prefer faster variants). We can configure at route-level in Console.

[06:00] Maya: we'll also show Console where you can pin model versions and change routing policies live.
[06:08] [06:08] Liam (screen): switching to Console — routes tab, model pins, fallback policy drop-down. you can see a recent canary rollout we ran where traffic split 95/5.
[06:25] Aisha: Do you expose token-level latency breakdowns? we need to show infra vs model time in our SRE dashboards.
[06:31] Liam: Yes. Console trace view shows token emission times and runtime kernel time. we give breakdowns for queue time, execution time, and network tail. exportable as CSV for your observability pipeline.

[07:00] Jon: back to retries: how do you avoid double-charges if we re-run a generation?
[07:05] Liam: We recommend client-side idempotency keys for create calls. server will detect duplicate idempotency keys within a time window and return previous response without recharging. for streaming replays with resume tokens you won't double charge for the same tokens if you resume correctly.

[07:30] Priya: What about rate limits? we have bursty traffic during business hours.
[07:34] Maya: Hosted API supports rate limiting per API key; we also offer quota-based tiers and soft-burst allowances. for predictable throughput at higher QPS you'd consider Redwood Dedicated but hosted can handle reasonable bursts with our autoscaling, though cold-start times vary by model.

[08:05] Aisha: Security: SSO/SCIM, KMS, logs — can we get your SOC 2 and encryption docs?
[08:11] Maya: yes. we'll attach SOC 2 summary and our security whitepaper. data at rest is encrypted with customer-managed KMS for Private deployments; for hosted we use provider-managed KMS but we can offer bring-your-own-key for Enterprise plans. audit logs and request-level metadata available in Console.

[08:45] Jon: Any differences in latency between models? we try to target 200-400ms p95 for short prompts.
[08:52] Liam: Absolutely. smaller models are way faster; your p95 will depend on context length and concurrency. with rwd-small and short prompts you'll see sub-200ms for single-request on GPU-backed endpoints typically, but under heavy concurrency queuing can push that up. we also have kernel-level optimizations (attention optimizations and kv cache reuse) that reduce per-token latency.

[09:25] [09:25] Liam (screen): Now quick demo of parameter tuning: I'll change temperature to 0.0 and then 0.7 to show output variance and token counts.
[09:40] [09:40] Liam: note when you lower max_tokens you may get truncated replies — stop sequences can help avoid that. also recommend deterministic seeds for testing: we expose a seed param in the SDK for repeatable results on some model families.

[10:10] Aisha: How do you recommend cost-control for chat sessions with long histories?
[10:15] Liam: Two levers: 1) prefix caching (we call it KV cache reuse) — if you reuse the conversation context you can avoid re-encoding earlier turns; 2) summarization + context windows — periodically summarize older turns to compress tokens. Console has an Optimize suggestion that flags high-cost routes and recommends batching or lower-precision quantized variants.

[10:45] Priya: Can you do server-side caching of responses for identical prompts?
[10:49] Liam: Yes — we support response caching by hash for deterministic calls (temp=0, same stop sequences). cache TTL configurable per-route.

[11:10] Jon: Outages: what's your fallback story if hosted region has intermittent issues?
[11:16] Liam: Smart routing supports multi-region fallback. policy options let you failover to another region or fallback to a cheaper but slower model. for strict data residency customers we can limit regions.

[11:40] Maya: Quick note: we logged a couple of common questions — we'll share a decision matrix for fallback vs retry.

[12:00] [12:00] Liam: I'm going to simulate a transient error now to show a retry with resume. watch the client logs.
[12:10] [12:10] Liam (screen): triggering error response 503 and client does exponential backoff. resumed request uses resume_cursor=45 and we only re-generate tokens after 45.
[12:30] Jon: Nice. that's helpful. any caveats?
[12:33] Liam: Caveat: if you change model or temperature mid-retry, resume may produce artifacts — best to preserve parameters during resume.

[13:00] Aisha: Team question — we have regulatory constraints, do you support data residency in EU only?
[13:07] Maya: Yes, hosted can be region-locked and we have EU region tenancy; for stricter needs Private deployment with on-prem is an option. we'll share a matrix of features by deployment type.

[13:35] Priya: For observability, can we stream audit logs into our SIEM?
[13:39] Liam: Yes, we support log export via S3/CloudWatch/Logstash and send event hooks for important lifecycle events.

[14:05] Jon: Anything about per-token pricing tiers? we'd like an idea of how pricing changes with model size.
[14:11] Maya: We'll send the pricing sheet. short answer: cost per token increases with model capacity; Redwood Optimize recommends lower-cost quantized variants for high-throughput use cases.

[14:35] [14:35] Liam: One more technical note: KV cache warms — if you do many similar requests we cache prefix encodings server-side to speed up subsequent calls in the same session. sometimes transcripts show 'KV cash' which is a funny transcription artifact.

[15:00] Aisha: Good to know. can you run a benchmark on our workload? we expect 500 QPS for short generation peaks but average 120 QPS.
[15:07] Maya: Yes. that's exactly what Liam will run — we'll use your prompt set and emulate 95/5 read/write chat behavior.

[15:30] Liam: For benchmarking we need: sample prompts, expected concurrency, desired p95 SLO, and whether you prefer latency or cost priority.

[15:45] Aisha: p95 300ms target, cost moderate, we'd rather have consistent latency than absolute lowest cost.

[16:00] Liam: Noted. we'll run hosted small/med, and a dedicated baseline if you'd like committed capacity numbers.

[16:20] Priya: Timeline: we want pilot in May. what's typical pilot timeline?
[16:24] Maya: Pilot can start within 2–3 weeks after paperwork; onboarding takes 1–2 weeks for keys, console access, and benchmarks.

[16:40] Jon: Any blocker around onboarding SSO? we use Okta.
[16:44] Maya: We support SAML SSO and SCIM for user provisioning. Okta is a common integration. for hosted we can enable it on your account once we have the enterprise agreement.

[17:05] Aisha: One more — how do you handle PII in prompts? we may process emails and names.
[17:10] Liam: For hosted we have redaction helpers and data retention controls; best practice is to token-mask PII client-side and use encryption in transit. for highest control, Private with customer-managed KMS is recommended.

[17:40] Priya: Are there SDK examples for resumable streaming in JS and Python?
[17:44] Liam: Yes — we'll share code snippets. the SDK has a StreamReader that exposes resume_cursor and reconnect logic.

[18:05] Maya: We're about 30 minutes in — maybe do a quick recap and next steps.
[18:12] Aisha: Sounds good.

[18:20] Maya: Recap: 1) Hosted API supports streaming with resume and SDK helpers, 2) recommended params for deterministic chat (temp 0-0.3, top_p ~0.9), 3) retries with exponential backoff + resume cursor for streaming, 4) fallback policies configurable in Console, 5) security docs and SOC 2 to be shared.

[18:45] Jon: That covers it. thanks.
[18:48] Maya: Action items: we'll send quickstart + pricing; Liam will run benchmarks once you share prompts; customer to confirm pilot week.

[19:05] Aisha: we'll aim to share the prompt set by Monday.
[19:09] Priya: ok. thanks everyone.
[19:12] Maya: Great. We'll follow up with calendar invites for the benchmark review and pilot kickoff.
[19:20] Jon: Thanks, bye.
[19:22] Liam: Thanks folks.

End of meeting.
